paragraphs.text: Polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic COL3A1 mutations. Affected individuals have specific structural brain anomalies, and some also have a severe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype. The brain phenotype is characterized by bilateral frontoparietal cobblestone polymicrogyria, cerebellar microcysts, and white matter abnormalities. It resembles the neurologic features of patients with autosomal recessive GPR56 mutations (Horn et al., 2017). The phenotype varies across patients (Vandervore et al., 2017).

paragraphs.text: Jørgensen et al. (2015) described a boy (III-2) who was born with right-sided clubfoot. He had a unilateral testicular hydrocele, crowded teeth, retrognathia, long slender fingers, and pale translucent skin. He died unexpectedly at age 15 years after a week of backache. At autopsy there were dissections of the thoracic aorta, the right renal artery, and the left femoral artery, with extensive bleeding and cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall. The brain looked normal macroscopically, but no brain imaging or histologic cerebral examination was performed. His sister (III-3) had long slender fingers, small-joint hypermobility, and translucent skin with visible veins. She also had the facial features of vascular EDS, spontaneous rupture of small superficial vessels, intermittent abdominal pain with blood in the stool, and migraine with aura. By age 19 to 20 years she had dissections of both internal carotid arteries and stenosis of the right external iliac artery, but her aortic dimensions were normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral thickened frontoparietal cortices with small gyri, consistent with pachy-micropolygyria. Despite this, her cognition and neurologic examination were normal, she had never had seizures, and her motor and language development had been normal.

paragraphs.text: Horn et al. (2017) described a 3-year-old girl with developmental delay who was born with bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, and dysmorphic facial features. At age 2 years she had an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage. Cerebral MRI showed a distinctive pattern of profound cerebral abnormalities, including bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone type. Horn et al. (2017) also described a second family in which 2 affected sibs had cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, white matter abnormalities, developmental delay, and seizures. The authors noted that 3 more families with biallelic COL3A1 variants had been reported previously. All of them had specific structural brain anomalies, and some had a severe EDS phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Jørgensen et al. (2015) found that 2 affected sibs were compound heterozygous for 2 COL3A1 variants. The first was a nonsense variant, c.1786C-T (R596X), in exon 26, which encodes part of the triple helical domain. The sibs had inherited it from their father, who was clinically unaffected at age 63. The second was a missense variant, c.3851G-A (G1284E), in exon 50, which encodes part of the C-terminal propeptide. The sibs had inherited it from their mother, who had only partial features of the disorder. The substituted glycine is highly conserved and lies next to a cysteine involved in interchain disulfide bonding, within a calcium-binding region. The authors predicted that the change would slow assembly of the trimer. An unaffected brother carried neither variant. The proband had no variants in the FBN1, TGFBR1, or TGFBR2 genes. Fibroblast studies showed reduced and overmodified type III procollagen in cells from the affected sister.

paragraphs.text: Jeong et al. (2012) found that Col3a1-null mice had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation. Its features were breakdown of the pial basement membrane (BM), neuronal overmigration, detachment of radial glial endfeet, and marginal zone heterotopias. All Col3a1-null mice examined at embryonic day (E) 18.5 had neuronal ectopias on the brain surface. The ectopias contained neurons from both deep and superficial cortical layers (Cux1+, Tbr1+, and CTIP2+), mirroring Gpr56-null mice. Ectopias were present in 23 of 28 null embryos, 0 of 12 heterozygotes, and 0 of 20 wildtype embryos. The pial BM formed normally at E10.5 despite the absence of collagen III. Regional breakdown of the BM with neuronal overmigration appeared in about half of E11.5 embryos and in all embryos older than E12.5. In the mutants, radial glial endfeet protruded through the breached BM, and Cajal-Retzius cells and calbindin-positive interneurons were misplaced into the ectopias.

paragraphs.text: In the sibs reported by Jørgensen et al. (2015), the second COL3A1 mutation was a c.3851G-A transition in exon 50, resulting in a gly1284-to-glu (G1284E) substitution in the C-terminal propeptide. The sibs had inherited it from their mother, who had only partial features of the disorder. The glycine is highly conserved and lies next to a cysteine involved in interchain disulfide bonding, within a calcium-binding region. The authors predicted that the change would slow assembly of the trimer. Cells from the mother made mostly normal type III procollagen plus a small amount of slightly overmodified procollagen. Cells from the compound heterozygous sister made a reduced amount of type III procollagen, and all of its chains were overmodified.

(2017) described a 3-year-old girl with developmental delay, bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, dysmorphic facial features, an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage at age 2 years, and bilateral frontoparietal cobblestone polymicrogyria. The other was a 1-bp deletion (c.2057delC).
